\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped, a dichotomy with a mechanistic basis.
Under nucleus sampling, top-$p$ truncation preserves the functional form of the conditional distribution at each step; what changes is the \emph{input}: as the model conditions on increasingly self-typical outputs, expected NLL compresses monotonically.
This yields two testable predictions: (1)~increasing sampling randomness should weaken the location drift, and (2)~semantic-preservation constraints should attenuate it.
Both are confirmed: at $t{=}1.0$, location signal collapses ($\rho$: $-0.60 \to -0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}); under elaboration prompts, drift weakens (F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
Causal analyses provide supporting evidence: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification, with 6/7 exhibiting significant Granger causality over the five-point chain, though the short series length (5 depths) limits formal causal inference (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
These results are established under nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$); shape features remain stable even at $\tau{=}1.0$ ($d < 0.15$; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).
Greedy decoding ($\tau{=}0$) confirms shape stability across all eight generators (mean $|d|{=}0.05$), establishing DDR as an autoregressive property independent of sampling truncation; top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$) compresses drifting effect sizes without introducing new shape instability, with boundary violations in Pythia/OLMo traceable to model-intrinsic baselines (Appendix~\ref{app:decoding-strategy}).

The classifier is a proof-of-concept for corpus-level auditing, not per-document filtering: gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for individual flagging but supports batch-level contamination estimation (${\pm}3$--$4$\% at $n{=}1{,}000$; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).
The three-class resolution enables depth-stratified corpus curation (retaining gen-1 content while flagging recursively degraded material), a distinction invisible to binary classifiers.
Depth-aware filtering can serve as a prophylactic against model collapse \cite{drayson_detection_prevents_collapse}, though depth-stratified curation does not yet improve downstream training (TOST equivalence at $\varepsilon{=}{\pm}2\%$; Appendix~\ref{app:downstream}); the primary value lies in provenance, not training improvement.

DDR is mechanistically distinct from model collapse \cite{curse_of_recursion,strong_model_collapse}: retraining erodes tail coverage by updating weights, whereas inference-chain drift at fixed parameters shifts only location, leaving shape stable.
Prior work establishes \emph{that} convergence occurs \cite{markovian_chains,curious_decline} without decomposing what drifts from what is preserved; DDR supplies this decomposition, isolating which distributional properties carry cross-generator depth signal, enabling detection without per-generator calibration.
Three depth classes define the practical resolution ceiling (5-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.50; Appendix~\ref{app:finer-depth}); QLoRA recovers more signal (F1\,=\,0.905, 6-gen LOGO; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), reflecting token-order patterns that aggregate statistics miss.
Instruction-tuned models compress DDR structure (3-class F1 degrades 3.7--19.9\,pp; Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), yet QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91, confirming token-level depth signal beyond summary-statistic decomposition.
Cross-domain evaluation (News, Academic, Code; $t{=}1.0$) yields binary F1\,=\,0.74--0.75 but degraded 3-class F1 (0.62--0.65; Appendix~\ref{app:domain}), with temperature and domain effects confounded.
Our generation chains use open-ended continuation prompts; real-world recursive pipelines (instruction-following chains, multi-turn dialogues, mixed-model editing) may attenuate, restructure, or introduce confounds not present in controlled chains.

4	\subsection{Depth Classification Performance}
5	\label{sec:results-classification}
6	
7	The 7-feature ensemble achieves 3-class LOGO F1\,=\,0.762 (95\% CI [0.758, 0.766]; $N$\,=\,37{,}058) across eight generators from five families (Table~\ref{tab:logo-results}), with cross-generator F1 spread of 9.1\,pp capturing generator selection uncertainty.
8	Because gen-0 seeds are shared across generators (\S\ref{sec:generation}), gen-0 classification is near-perfect (per-class F1\,$\approx$\,0.94), inflating the 3-class metric.
9	We therefore adopt \textbf{leak-free binary F1} (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+)\,=\,0.694 (CI [0.688, 0.700]) as the primary metric throughout: it excludes gen-0 entirely and is unaffected by seed sharing.
10	Per-generator binary F1 ranges from 0.633 (Mistral-7B) to 0.724 (Pythia-2.8B; SD\,=\,0.028), with the primary difficulty concentrated at the gen-1\,/\,gen-2+ boundary (Appendix~\ref{app:confusion}).
11	CIs reflect bootstrap sampling variability; the cross-generator range (9.1\,pp) captures the distinct and larger uncertainty of generator selection.
12	
13	\paragraph{Cross-model generalization.}
14	Cross-model chains (randomly selected generator per step) yield binary F1\,=\,0.830 (95\% CI [.818, .841]) under 5-generator LOGO.\footnote{5-generator subset (Pythia-2.8B/1B, OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B/1.7B); generator-level LOGO with bootstrap CIs ($n$\,=\,2{,}000). Not directly comparable to 8-generator LOGO due to differing subsets.}
15	Single-generator transfer (Appendix~\ref{app:transfer}) establishes that the signal is not a mixed-chain artifact: classifiers trained on one generator transfer to all others with mean binary F1\,=\,0.810; LOFO yields 0.686.
16	A scale effect emerges: Pythia achieves the highest F1 (0.718--0.724) while larger models degrade (Mistral-7B: 0.633), partly reflecting same-family affinity with the Pythia-410M reference (cross-reference spread $\leq$0.013; \S\ref{sec:results-differential}); cross-domain signal persists with variation (Appendix~\ref{app:domain}).
17	An end-to-end QLoRA classifier achieves 3-class F1\,=\,0.905 under 6-generator LOGO ($+$11.6\,pp vs.\ the same-subset XGBoost baseline of 0.789; Appendix~\ref{app:qlora}), confirming that richer token-level representations capture additional depth signal; on instruct data, QLoRA recovers to 0.89--0.91 within-model (Appendix~\ref{app:instruct}), establishing the empirical decomposition, not the specific classifier, as DDR's primary contribution.
18	
19	\paragraph{Length confound control.}
20	Length-matched subsampling yields binary F1\,=\,0.724 (vs.\ 0.770 unmatched); a random-subsample control verifies the drop reflects deconfounding, not sample-size reduction (Appendix~\ref{app:length}).
21	
22	\paragraph{Seed-sharing control.}
23	Seed-level demeaning (F1\,=\,0.701) and an independent-seed experiment with disjoint seed pools (F1\,=\,0.680; Appendix~\ref{app:seed-control}) both verify that the classifier captures generative degradation, not seed-specific content.

50	\subsection{Differential Depth Response}
51	\label{sec:results-differential}
52	
53	\begin{figure*}[t]
54	\centering
55	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_ddr_trajectory.pdf}
56	\caption{Feature trajectories across generation depth. \textbf{Top row (drifting)}: entropy mean and hapax ratio decline monotonically across all eight generators ($|\rho| > 0.59$). \textbf{Bottom row (stationary)}: entropy max and tail decay remain flat ($|\rho| < 0.07$). Colored lines: individual generators; diamonds: cross-generator mean (blue for drifting, amber for stationary). This dichotomy defines the differential depth response (DDR).}
57	\label{fig:ddr-trajectory}
58	\end{figure*}
59	
60	Recursive generation does not affect all distributional properties uniformly.
61	Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-trajectory} exposes a consistent dichotomy across all eight generators: central-tendency features (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio) decline monotonically with depth, while shape features (entropy max, tail decay, entropy min) remain flat.
62	This asymmetry constitutes the \emph{differential depth response} (DDR).
63	The primary partition is binary: $k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space yields silhouette\,=\,0.660 (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}), cleanly separating three \emph{drifting} features ($|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) from four \emph{non-drifting} ones ($d \leq 0.55$); higher $k$ degrades cluster quality ($k{=}3$: silhouette\,=\,0.532).
64	A domain-informed refinement resolves entropy std as a sole \emph{intermediate} member ($d{=}0.55$, $|\rho|{=}0.16$), distinct from the three near-stationary features ($d < 0.10$; CV shift $<$3\% vs.\ $>$15\% for drifting features).
65	Multiple effect-size measures corroborate this partition, establishing that the asymmetry reflects distributional structure rather than feature-selection artifact (Quantification below).
66	
67	\begin{figure}[t!]
68	\centering
69	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig1_differential_response.pdf}
70	\caption{Differential depth response (DDR). Diamonds: cross-generator means; dots: per-generator values. Drifting features (blue; $|\rho| > 0.60$, $d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) show strong monotonic depth sensitivity; non-drifting features remain stable. Entropy std (wine; $d{=}0.55$) is an intermediate member; near-stationary features (amber; $d \leq 0.10$) show negligible drift. Entropy min ($|\rho|{=}0.40$ pooled; gen-0/gen-1 sensitive) and tail decay (TOST 4/8) are boundary features within this group.}
71	\label{fig:feature-drift}
72	\end{figure}
73	
74	Pooled class-balanced Spearman correlations with depth corroborate the binary split (Figure~\ref{fig:feature-drift}):
75	drifting features show substantial monotonic trends (hapax ratio $\rho = -0.64$, TTR $\rho = -0.63$, entropy mean $\rho = -0.60$),
76	while non-drifting features remain near-zero (tail decay $|\rho| = 0.04$; per-depth distributions in Appendix~\ref{app:feature-distributions}).
77	The six-fold magnitude gap between drifting ($|\rho| > 0.60$) and non-drifting features ($|\rho| \leq 0.16$) defines the DDR partition.
78	Within the non-drifting group, entropy std ($|\rho| = 0.16$, $d{=}0.55$) shows a substantial level shift despite low monotonicity, distinguishing it from the three near-stationary features ($d < 0.10$); this refinement is stable across $d$ thresholds in $[0.56, 0.75]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
79	
80	\paragraph{Quantification.}
81	Parametric and non-parametric effect-size measures converge on the split.
82	Cohen's $d$ \cite{cohen1988statistical} shows a ${\geq}7\times$ gap between drifting ($d{=}0.76$--$1.17$) and near-stationary features ($d \leq 0.08$); KS statistics, Glass's $\Delta$, Cliff's $\delta$, and CV shift all corroborate (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
83	Four features fall cleanly into drifting or non-drifting groups.
84	Entropy min and tail decay are \emph{boundary features}: entropy min is near-stationary for gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+ ($d{=}0.016$) but sensitive at gen-0/gen-1 ($|\rho|{=}0.40$); tail decay is \emph{weakly stationary}, passing TOST for only 4/8 generators ($|d|{=}0.10$--$0.22$).
85	Entropy std ($d{=}0.55$, $|\rho|{=}0.16$) is the sole intermediate member.
86	\paragraph{Validation.}
87	Per-generator split analysis provides the strongest validation: each of the eight hold-out generators independently recovers the identical drifting/non-drifting partition (per-generator silhouette range 0.505--0.760; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
88	$k{=}2$ clustering in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space corroborates this separation (silhouette\,=\,0.660), invariant across threshold choices $\varepsilon \in [0.10, 0.75]$.
89	Per-generator TOST equivalence testing ($\varepsilon{=}|d|{<}0.20$, following Cohen's~\citeyearpar{cohen1988statistical} conventional threshold; gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+) confirms near-stationarity for entropy min (8/8 pass) and entropy max (6/8); tail decay passes for only 4/8, with $|d|{=}0.10$--$0.22$ spanning the boundary.
90	A permutation test ($n{=}10{,}000$) establishes the three-vs-four split as non-random ($p{=}0.030$; fixed-label silhouette\,=\,0.660 vs.\ null mean\,=\,0.46); exhaustive enumeration of all $\binom{7}{3}{=}35$ possible splits ranks this partition first (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-validation}).
91	Reclassifying either boundary feature as intermediate preserves the core drifting/non-drifting split and leaves classification unchanged.
92	
93	\paragraph{Feature complementarity.}
94	The full 7-feature set (F1\,=\,0.773, 10-fold stratified CV) outperforms surface-only (0.688) and reference-only (0.713; McNemar $p \approx 0$; Appendix~\ref{app:ablation-table}).
95	PCA confirms the three drifting features share a single latent dimension (92.3\% variance; Appendix~\ref{sec:appendix-feature-correlation}); replacing them with PC1 costs only 1.1\,pp, reinforcing that DDR's contribution is identifying \emph{which} distributional properties drift, not classification per se.
96	TTR and hapax ratio ($r = 0.97$) are both retained for marginal LOFO gains despite feature masking \cite{strobl_conditional_2008} (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}).
97	
98	\paragraph{Cross-family reference models.}
99	Alternative references (OLMo-2-1B, Qwen3-0.6B) achieve comparable LOGO F1 (spread 0.013; Appendix~\ref{app:cross-ref}), bounding the same-family affinity effect; depth features are robust to reference model choice, though residual same-family proximity may inflate Pythia-family F1 by up to 1.3\,pp.
100	
101	\paragraph{Temperature and prompt-type sensitivity.}
102	All four tested generators degrade at $t{=}0.9$ ($-9.3$ to $-26.0$\,pp binary F1); low-temperature improvement is family-dependent ($+7$--$9$\,pp for Pythia/OLMo at $t{=}0.5$, negligible for Qwen; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}).
103	Continuation chains show the strongest drift (F1\,=\,0.781), with cross-prompt-type transfer confirming shared signal (LOPTO F1\,=\,0.753; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}); the DDR partition hierarchy is preserved across temperatures despite absolute effect-size compression (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).
104	
105	
106	\subsection{Comparison with Detection Baselines}
107	\label{sec:results-baselines}
108	
109	Existing detection methods target binary real-vs-synthetic classification; we test whether their continuous scores incidentally encode recursive depth by repurposing four detection scores as ordinal depth predictors under identical XGBoost and LOGO conditions (Table~\ref{tab:baselines}).

Inference costs measured on a single NVIDIA RTX 5090.}
136	\label{fig:baseline-ci}
137	\end{figure}
138	
139	The 7-feature ensemble surpasses all individual baselines in 3-class F1 ($\Delta$\,=\,6.7--36.3\,pp; Figure~\ref{fig:baseline-ci}) and the pure 4-detector ensemble in binary F1 (0.705 vs.\ 0.700).
140	Adding DDR's surface features to the four detectors yields the highest binary F1 (0.708), marginally above the 7-feature set at 2.4$\times$ the inference cost.
141	This result underscores that DDR's primary contribution is not classification performance (multi-detector ensembles match or marginally exceed it) but the decomposition of depth signal into location-sensitive and shape-stable components, a structural distinction absent from both binary detection methods and model collapse analyses (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\label{app:tost}

To confirm that the near-stationary classification is not a pooling artifact, we apply two one-sided $t$-tests (TOST) \cite{lakens_equivalence} for each feature within each generator separately (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, equivalence bound $|d| < 0.20$).

LOFO analysis independently supports this choice: removing any near-stationary feature changes classification F1 by $\leq$1.5\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}), linking the statistical threshold to classification irrelevance.
Sensitivity analysis at $\varepsilon \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25\}$ confirms the partition is robust to the bound choice (see DDR Validation appendix).
Table~\ref{tab:tost-per-gen} reports observed $|d|$; \checkmark{} marks features for which the TOST null hypothesis (non-equivalence) is rejected at $\alpha = 0.05$.

All drifting and intermediate features fail equivalence uniformly, with $|d|$ ranging from 0.23 (entropy std, Mistral) to 1.40 (entropy mean, Pythia-1B).
The partition is robust at the individual-generator level, with entropy min as the most consistently stationary feature.

Three-class classification is more sensitive (0.737$\to$0.367 at 20\%), because distinguishing gen-0 from gen-1 relies heavily on lexical diversity features (TTR, hapax ratio) that are directly disrupted by word replacement.
The binary metric, which excludes gen-0, is inherently more robust since it depends primarily on reference-model entropy features distributed across many tokens.

\paragraph{Feature subset degradation.}
Table~\ref{tab:feature-degrade} compares perturbation robustness of the full 7-feature ensemble against an entropy-only subset (5 reference-model features).
The higher unperturbed binary F1 of the entropy-only subset (0.833 vs.\ 0.695) reflects the strong discriminability of reference-model features for the coarse binary task (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+); however, lexical features are essential for the finer-grained ordinal task (3-class F1: 0.737 vs.\ 0.688) and provide greater robustness under perturbation.
At 20\% replacement, the 7-feature ensemble surpasses entropy-only on binary F1 (0.591 vs.\ 0.569), despite starting from a lower baseline.
Random word replacement drastically alters per-token context and makes entropy features (computed over the full token sequence) extremely sensitive to noise.
Lexical features (TTR, hapax ratio), as document-level summary statistics, are more stable under per-word perturbation and act as stabilizers in the full ensemble.
The crossover confirms that degradation in the full feature set reflects genuine signal disruption rather than a lexical-feature artifact.

\small

5\%  & 0.738 & 0.650 & 0.539 & 0.641 \\

20\% & 0.569 & 0.591 & 0.314 & 0.367 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Baseline comparison.}
Table~\ref{tab:baseline-robustness} compares robustness across detection methods under identical perturbation conditions (8-gen LOGO, binary: gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+).

\begin{table}[ht]
\centering
\small
\caption{Baseline robustness under random word replacement (8-gen LOGO, binary F1). Bold indicates highest F1 at each perturbation rate.}
\label{tab:baseline-robustness}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
\textbf{Method} & \textbf{0\%} & \textbf{5\%} & \textbf{10\%} & \textbf{20\%} \\
\midrule
7-feature ensemble & \textbf{0.695} & 0.650 & 0.614 & 0.591 \\
LD-Score           & 0.677 & \textbf{0.673} & \textbf{0.677} & \textbf{0.671} \\
Avg-LogProb        & 0.682 & 0.419 & 0.335 & 0.375 \\
FastDetectGPT      & 0.571 & 0.437 & 0.468 & 0.514 \\
Binoculars\textsuperscript{\dag}         & 0.500 & 0.461 & 0.446 & 0.425 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}

\vspace{2pt}
{\footnotesize \textsuperscript{\dag}Binoculars operates at chance level on this binary task; its degradation figures are not meaningful.}
\end{table}

The 7-feature ensemble achieves the highest unperturbed binary F1 (0.695), but LD-Score surpasses it under perturbation due to near-zero degradation ($-$0.6\,pp across the full 0\%$\to$20\% range).
FastDetectGPT and Avg-LogProb exhibit non-monotonic degradation at higher perturbation rates, likely because severe perturbation introduces distributional artifacts that these token-level methods detect as anomalous.
Avg-LogProb is the most fragile overall ($-$34.7\,pp at 10\%), while FastDetectGPT drops sharply at 5\% ($-$13.4\,pp) before partially recovering.
LD-Score is nearly invariant to perturbation, consistent with its reliance on corpus-level distributional divergence rather than per-token likelihoods.
The 7-feature ensemble offers the highest starting performance among single-reference methods, with sublinear degradation ($-$10.4\,pp at 20\%).

\paragraph{LLM-simulated sentence regeneration.}
To test robustness under semantically coherent editing, we use Qwen3-0.6B-Base to randomly regenerate 1--3 sentences per passage (avg 1.69 sentences, ${\sim}$50\% edit distance) and re-evaluate the 8-gen LOGO pipeline.
Binary F1 drops from 0.692 to 0.647 ($-$4.5\,pp, 6.5\% relative); 3-class F1 drops from 0.739 to 0.667 ($-$7.1\,pp, 9.7\% relative).
The binary degradation ($-$4.5\,pp) is nearly identical to that caused by 5\% random word replacement ($-$4.6\,pp), despite the LLM rephrase altering ${\sim}$50\% of characters.
This asymmetry arises because LLM-generated replacements preserve the underlying statistical signature of the generation process (entropy dynamics, depth-accumulated distributional drift), whereas random word substitution directly destroys local statistical signals.
Depth profiling thus captures deep generative structure that survives semantic-preserving edits.

\paragraph{Seed complexity.}
Performance is stable across seed text complexity: stratifying seeds by vocabulary richness (TTR terciles) yields maximum F1 variation of 1.1\,pp across groups.

\paragraph{Per-generator replication.}
To rule out the possibility that the pooled silhouette is an artifact of mixing heterogeneous generators, we repeat the $(|\rho|, d)$ clustering independently for each of the eight generators.
Every generator recovers the identical \{$\bar{H}$, TTR, hapax\} vs.\ \{$\sigma_H$, $H_{\min}$, $H_{\max}$, tail\} partition, with silhouette scores ranging from 0.505 (Pythia-1B) to 0.760 (Mistral-7B-v0.3; mean\,=\,0.651).
No generator falls below the 0.50 moderate-structure threshold, confirming that the two-cluster structure is a per-generator property rather than a pooling artifact.

\subsection*{TOST Equivalence Bound Sensitivity}
\label{app:tost-sensitivity}

Table~\ref{tab:tost-sensitivity} shows the fraction of generators for which each feature passes the TOST equivalence test (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, $\alpha{=}0.05$) at three equivalence bounds $\varepsilon$.

\centering
\small
\caption{TOST equivalence pass rate across 8 generators at varying $\varepsilon$.}
\label{tab:tost-sensitivity}

\textbf{DDR Zone} & \textbf{Feature} & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.15}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.20}$ & $\boldsymbol{\varepsilon{=}0.25}$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{3}{*}{Drifting} & $\bar{H}$ (ent.\ mean) & 0/8 & 0/8 & 0/8 \\

\bottomrule
\end{tabular}}
\end{table}

The partition is robust to the equivalence bound: drifting features reject equivalence at all $\varepsilon$ for all generators, while entropy min passes even at the stricter bound $\varepsilon{=}0.15$ (7/8 generators).
Tail decay is the most $\varepsilon$-sensitive near-stationary feature, passing 4/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.20$ but 7/8 at $\varepsilon{=}0.25$; the four non-passing generators show $|d|{=}0.15$--$0.22$, still well below the drifting threshold ($d > 0.50$).

\paragraph{Threshold sensitivity.}
To address concerns about the sensitivity of the drifting-boundary threshold,
we sweep $|d|$ from $0.10$ to $0.80$ in increments of $0.05$ and record the
resulting binary partition (drifting vs.\ stationary) along with the silhouette
score in standardized $(|\rho|, d)$ space.
Across the entire range, only \emph{three} distinct partitions emerge,
reflecting natural gaps between feature clusters rather than threshold artifacts.
The three-feature drifting set (entropy mean, TTR, hapax ratio)
is stable across $|d| \in [0.50,\, 0.75]$ with a silhouette of $0.660$---the
peak value in the sweep.
Including the intermediate feature entropy std ($d{=}0.49$) yields a
4/3 partition stable across $|d| \in [0.10,\, 0.45]$ (silhouette\,=\,0.451).
The partition used in our analysis corresponds to the peak-silhouette region,
confirming that the drifting/stationary boundary reflects a natural gap in the
$(|\rho|, d)$ landscape rather than an artifact of a particular
threshold choice.

\paragraph{Partition stability across $\varepsilon$ thresholds.}
\label{app:epsilon-sweep}

\label{app:holdout-split}

\label{app:heteroscedasticity}

\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}

Recursive generation alters \emph{where} the token-level surprise distribution sits but not \emph{how} it is shaped, a dichotomy with a mechanistic basis.
Under nucleus sampling, top-$p$ truncation preserves the functional form of the conditional distribution at each step; what changes is the \emph{input}: as the model conditions on increasingly self-typical outputs, expected NLL compresses monotonically.
This yields two testable predictions: (1)~increasing sampling randomness should weaken the location drift, and (2)~semantic-preservation constraints should attenuate it.
Both are confirmed: at $t{=}1.0$, location signal collapses ($\rho$: $-0.60 \to -0.002$; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling-sensitivity}); under elaboration prompts, drift weakens (F1\,=\,0.730 vs.\ 0.781; Appendix~\ref{app:prompt-type}).
Causal analyses provide supporting evidence: drifting features contribute $5.5\times$ more to classification, with 6/7 exhibiting significant Granger causality over the five-point chain, though the short series length (5 depths) limits formal causal inference (Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-causality}).
These results are established under nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.95$); shape features remain stable even at $\tau{=}1.0$ ($d < 0.15$; Appendix~\ref{app:ddr-temp-stability}).
Greedy decoding ($\tau{=}0$) confirms shape stability across all eight generators (mean $|d|{=}0.05$), establishing DDR as an autoregressive property independent of sampling truncation; top-$k$ sampling ($k{=}50$) compresses drifting effect sizes without introducing new shape instability, with boundary violations in Pythia/OLMo traceable to model-intrinsic baselines (Appendix~\ref{app:decoding-strategy}).

The classifier is a proof-of-concept for corpus-level auditing, not per-document filtering: gen-1 per-class F1\,=\,0.63 is insufficient for individual flagging but supports batch-level contamination estimation (${\pm}3$--$4$\% at $n{=}1{,}000$; Appendix~\ref{app:error-analysis}).

\section{Per-Generator Equivalence Testing}
\label{app:tost}

To confirm that the near-stationary classification is not a pooling artifact, we apply two one-sided $t$-tests (TOST) \cite{lakens_equivalence} for each feature within each generator separately (gen-1 vs.\ gen-2+, equivalence bound $|d| < 0.20$).
We adopt Cohen's conventional small effect size ($d{=}0.20$) \cite{cohen1988statistical} as the smallest effect of practical significance (SESOI): effects below this threshold are unlikely to be practically meaningful for depth discrimination.
LOFO analysis independently supports this choice: removing any near-stationary feature changes classification F1 by $\leq$1.5\,pp (Appendix~\ref{app:lofo}), linking the statistical threshold to classification irrelevance.
Sensitivity analysis at $\varepsilon \in \{0.15, 0.20, 0.25\}$ confirms the partition is robust to the bound choice (see DDR Validation appendix).
Table~\ref{tab:tost-per-gen} reports observed $|d|$; \checkmark{} marks features for which the TOST null hypothesis (non-equivalence) is rejected at $\alpha = 0.05$.

Entropy min passes equivalence for all eight generators; entropy max passes for six of eight (exceeding $\varepsilon$ only for Pythia-1B and Pythia-2.8B, where $|d| \approx 0.21$--$0.25$); tail decay passes for four of eight.
All drifting and intermediate features fail equivalence uniformly, with $|d|$ ranging from 0.23 (entropy std, Mistral) to 1.40 (entropy mean, Pythia-1B).
The partition is robust at the individual-generator level, with entropy min as the most consistently stationary feature.
Figure~\ref{fig:ddr-scatter} visualizes the DDR partition in ($|\rho|$, $d$) space, showing a clear gap between the three groups.
